theme: The Temple built, the permanent dwelling of God
readingInstruction: Read 1 Kings 6:1-7:51. The temple is built. Read the details as a description of a house for God’s presence, and watch for the note in 6:11-13, where God speaks.
settingTheScene: Solomon begins to build the temple in the fourth year of his reign, 480 years after the exodus. The temple is on Mount Moriah, the threshing floor David had purchased. The design follows that of the tabernacle but is larger and more permanent. The chapters also describe Solomon’s palace and the bronze work of Hiram. It was a seven-year project.
observation: “In the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt… he began to build the house of the LORD” (6:1).
The stones were prepared at the quarry, “so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built” (6:7).
God’s word comes to Solomon: “Concerning this house that you are building, if you will walk in my statutes… then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father” (6:11-13).
“And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel” (6:13).
The inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place, is a cube, overlaid with gold, with two cherubim of olive wood (6:19-28).
The walls are carved with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers (6:29-35).
“He was seven years in building it” (6:38).
Solomon spent thirteen years building his own house (7:1).
interpretation:
The temple is a work of extraordinary care. Even its construction was done in reverence: stones cut at the quarry, so that no hammering was heard at the site. It reflects the holiness of the place. The temple’s carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers recall the garden of Eden. The temple is a miniature Eden: a place where God dwells with his people. The Most Holy Place, a perfect cube covered in gold, is later echoed in the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:16).

In the middle of the building account, God speaks. It is a short but important interruption. The temple is not enough. The building is secondary to obedience. “If you will walk in my statutes… then I will establish my word with you.” The promise of dwelling among them is tied to faithfulness. The temple could not save Israel if they were not obedient. This is the theme the prophets would later echo (Jeremiah 7:4).

The detail that it took seven years to build the temple and thirteen to build his own house is probably a quiet comment. The narrator does not accuse. But the contrast gives the reader pause. Where do a king’s priorities lie? Over time, the palace would grow while devotion declined.

The bronze work of Hiram, with the two pillars Jachin and Boaz, the sea, and the ten basins, shows the grandeur. The pillars’ names mean “he establishes” and “in him is strength.” They stood at the entrance as a statement about where Israel’s security lay.

The temple is a beautiful thing. But the people of God needed to learn that God does not live in houses made with hands. He chose to dwell there, but he cannot be contained by it.
connection: Jesus is the true temple (John 2:19-21), the place where God dwells with man (John 1:14). Believers are now God’s temple, built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21-22). Stephen reminded his hearers that “the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands” (Acts 7:48). Revelation 21:22 says of the New Jerusalem, “I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.”
application:
Reflect on the proportion between how much you invest in your own house and in God’s.

Remember that you are now a temple of the Holy Spirit. How does that shape how you live?

Thank God for the Eden-like promise of dwelling with his people.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for making his dwelling with his people.
Thank him that you are a dwelling place for his Spirit.
Ask him to keep you from building your own house before his.
